newsitem.title: USA: CIA agent indicted on charges of spying for Russia.
newsitem.headline: CIA agent indicted on charges of spying for Russia.

text.p: A federal grand jury on Thursday indicted CIA employee Harold Nicholson on charges of conspiring to spy for Russia and prosecutors sought to recover almost $200,000 in proceeds from his alleged espionage.

The formal indictment, announced by the Justice Department, mirrored the charges made in a criminal complaint earlier this week, alleging that Nicholson -- a CIA employee since 1982 -- conspired to violate U.S. espionage laws by passing classified information to the Russians.

According to the indictment, Nicholson "delivered to the Russian Federation documents, photographic negatives and information relating to the national defence of the United States" from June 1994 through November 16, 1996.
It alleges that as recently as 10 days ago, Nicholson requested and obtained a document camera from the CIA's technical services department.

"On or about November 12 and continuing through November 15, 1996, Nicholson, using the CIA document camera, photographed classified documents relating to the national defence of the United States, with the intent to transmit and deliver those photographs to agents of the Russian Federation in Zurich, Switzerland during his upcoming trip," the indictment said.
Nicholson was arrested by the Federal Bureau of Investigation last Saturday at Washington's Dulles Airport as he was about to fly to Switzerland.

He had been an operations officer in various posts around the world and worked as an instructor at a classified training centre for CIA undercover operatives in Virginia during the time he is accused of spying.

The indictment also alleged that Nicholson compiled national defence information on his personal notebook computer for transmission to Russian agents and that using the code name "Nevil R. Strachey" he communicated with his handlers by mailing postcards to a post office box in a foreign country.
During twice-yearly meetings outside the United States, in places such as Malaysia, Thailand and Singapore, Nicholson transmitted information to Russian agents, it said.

The indictment alleged that Nicholson received "sums exceeding $180,000" from Russian agents in return for classified information. The Justice Department said if Nicholson were convicted on the sole count, it would seek to recover $180,000 in U.S. currency, a Chevrolet Lumina Sports Van and a Toshiba notebook computer.
The charge against Nicholson carries a possible sentence of life in prison without parole. Prosecutors said the case so far did not meet requirements for seeking the death penalty.
Although a formal plea has not been entered, Nicholson's attorney has said his client would plead not guilty.
